GTA 6 leaks show a game that looks like more GTA, but not a revolution
summary: It sure doesn't look like the reinvention of the wheel(s).
body: The exciting thing about Rockstar games is not that they have the most advanced technology behind them, the best stories, or the most avant-garde game systems. It's the extraordinary amount of work the studio invests into the little details that make up its big worlds. Red Dead Redemption's dynamic horse testicles (they shrink when it's cold) are a frequently-cited example of that commitment to the particulars. A pair of videos purported to be leaked GTA 6 gameplay surfaced online today , and if they are legit (the immediate copyright takedowns suggest as much), they seem to confirm that GTA 6 is more of the same. The short clips obviously can't express the full scope of Rockstar's designs—and we don't know how recent they are—but there's nothing in them to indicate that GTA 6 will reinvent the open-world crime spree. In one, the player shoots some hoops as protagonist Jason. It's cool that a basketball on the ground and a hoop nailed to the side of your house are not just static props. There's a system in place for shooting accurately, and the game tracks the number of shots made. The other clip is a very typical GTA scene: The player makes a reckless turn in a car, gets clipped …

title: Industry legend Warren Spector is retiring: 'I'm feeling like I've done what I set out to do'
summary: The man who helped give us Ultima Underworld, System Shock, Deus Ex, and Epic Mickey is riding off into the sunset.
body: Warren Spector is one of the industry's most storied developers, particularly among fans of immersive sims. His leading roles on games like Ultima Underworld , System Shock , and Deus Ex —and you know what, even Invisible War and Deadly Shadows , which are probably better than you think—established him as one of the field's most admired and enduring names. And now, after doing it for more than 40 years, he's calling it a day. "Let me cut right to the chase. I'm retiring from game development," Spector wrote on LinkedIn . "At least I think so. I've been here before and changed my mind but this time I'm pretty sure I mean it." Spector said he's had a "great career" and wouldn't change a thing, but added that he's coming up on 44 years as a developer, a span that's seen him work on tabletop RPGs, board games, and "more digital games than [he] can remember," as part of teams ranging in size from a dozen people to 800. "I've worked for big companies and done startups," he wrote. "I like to think I've helped some insanely talented people along in their careers. (That last is the most important.) "With all that behind me and with age and health (my business) catching up with me I'm feeli…

title: 'Live-service is a red flag for us': Why one publisher is embracing an older kind of multiplayer hit: peer-to-peer, server browsers, and organic community
summary: Tripwire sees preservation as a responsibility.
body: It's a frustrating thing to watch good games disappear. We've seen it happen time and time and time again: studios spend years on a cool multiplayer thing, bank on it being popular enough to become a live-service hit, then toss the entire project into the trash when that doesn't happen. That could have been the fate of Deceive Inc , a 2023 'PvP Hitman' shooter that has attracted a passionate, but small community. Developer Sweet Bandits supported the game with substantial updates and microtransactions for over a year, but unfortunately shut down in 2024, leaving fans to assume Deceive Inc would one day disappear, too. Then last month, the unexpected happened : an update on its Steam page announced that not only would Deceive Inc not be going offline, but work is underway on community server tools and mod support that will essentially give the game to the community, and keep it playable forever. The update is not the work of Sweet Bandits, but an initiative of Deceive Inc's publisher, Tripwire Interactive. title: 2 seemingly real GTA 6 clips—and maybe the full map—just leaked online
summary: B-b-b-b-b-basketball.
body: Two seemingly genuine Grand Theft Auto 6 gameplay clips are making the rounds online. The first, a minute-long clip originally posted by a group or individual named "Cyberleek", is already being reposted in multiple places, but we first noticed it via gaming forum ResetEra . As of writing, the clip already has more than 100,000 views. In the clip, we see protagonist Jason Duval at an oceanside house—the same one that we've seen in trailers. The player jumps over his deck and onto the driveway, where he picks up a basketball and shoots some hoops. For sinking a basket, the player increases their "Focus" by 2%. We see two cash totals listed in the HUD—presumably one for their on-hand cash, and one for their bank. Another clip, posted almost an hour later, shows the player driving around a beat-up car, crashing into a delivery truck, and then attacking the driver. Elsewhere, Cyberleek has also published supposed screenshots of the in-game map, though art has appears too simple to be how it will actually look in the game. title: Epic Mickey creator Warren Spector is 'a little bitter' that his studio isn't getting props for sparking Oswald the Lucky Rabbit's big comeback
summary: Oswald, who featured in both Epic Mickey games, is getting an animated miniseries in 2027, and Spector rightly thinks his team should get credit for helping make it happen.
body: Epic Mickey man Warren Spector—also known for other games you may have heard of, like Ultima Underworld, System Shock, and Deus Ex—recently took to LinkedIn to share some thoughts about Disney's upcoming Oswald the Lucky Rabbit miniseries, which was showcased by Jon Favreau at the recent D23 event. Spector said he's "seriously looking forward to it," but he's also a little annoyed by what he sees as the erasure of the game that helped bring the character back into the public consciousness. Favreau provided a brief overview of Oswald's creation in the 1920s during his presentation, relating how creator Walt Disney lost the rights to the character shortly thereafter. While numerous Oswald shorts were produced, the character was utterly overshadowed by Disney's subsequent creation, Mickey Mouse, and languished in obscurity for years. Disney reacquired the rights to Oswald in 2006, and "we've seen him pop up in games and in shorts and things" since then, Favreau said—and, well, that's the extent of it. That didn't sit right with Spector, who made Oswald a major NPC in Epic Mickey, and a playable character in Epic Mickey 2: The Power of Two. "I’m seriously looking forward to it but it …

body: Grand Theft Auto 6 will, I'm assured, be the most immersive videogame of all time. You simply won't be able to discern reality from fiction anymore. title: Star Wars: Galactic Racer's multiplayer 'tour' mode is a chaotic arcade racer spliced with a MOBA, and that somehow works brilliantly
summary: Going on tour.
body: I had the pleasure of playing Star Wars: Galactic Racer recently —it's an upcoming racing game by Fuse Games, a studio filled with Burnout alumni, and while I was intrigued by the roguelike elements of its singleplayer campaign, the real standout to me is its online multiplayer, which is doing something that I would otherwise call ill-advised: Making it a MOBA. Sort of. When I say the mode's been spliced with a MOBA, I mean that a ton of elements—buildcrafting, match-specific progression, and personal player economy (the more credits you get, the faster you'll scale over the competition)—are similar. It's a little like Overwatch's Stadium mode, which used a lot of familiar MOBA itemisation without the inclusion of lanes or towers. Now, to be clear, there will be online modes without any of these elements—but given it was the mode Fuse had me playing, the "tour" mode was clearly the one Fuse Games is the most eager to show off. And I can see why, it's genuinely unique. Here's how it works: 12 players (or eight, if you're doing podracing) fight across six planets. title: Post Malone breaks into his $2 million The One Ring, stressing out a whole room of Magic: The Gathering players: 'our insurance doesn't cover that card'
summary: This is a rich person bit I'm too poor to understand.
body: My biggest financial blunder occurred at the ripe old age of six. It wasn't failing to buy up property in 2008, nor was it failing to swipe a popular domain name, although those probably would have come in handy. No, the mistake that haunts my nightmares was six year old Elie bringing an immaculate Umbreon Undaunted holo to the playground, despite my dad telling me not to because it was pretty and I wanted to show my friends. It's been downhill since then. Bear in mind this is just a $20,000 card which has since been chewed up and spat out. But in the high stakes world of TCG it barely compares, especially not against Magic: The Gathering's exclusive The One Ring card—part of a Lord of the Rings crossover expansion—which is valued at an eye-watering $2 million . So you can imagine my horror when I saw its owner, Post Malone , bring it out during a MTG Commander session and then proceed to tear into its casing. "I'm taking it out of the obnoxious big block, it would ruin Game Knights," Posty says while popping the lid during Game Knights on The Command Zone . title: The RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB currently costs more than the RTX 5070 and RX 9070 XT, and I know which one I'd pick
summary: Graphics card prices are surging, but GeForce cards have been hit hardest.
body: Prices for graphics cards are still on the rise. Just last week, we noted prices were at the worst we've seen them in the past 12 months , but after further checks this morning, they're looking worse again still. Among the worst offenders, the RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB . With memory being the main driving factor of price hikes in the past 12 months, it's perhaps no surprise that this memory-laden card is rising faster than most. Yet prices are beyond the pale. In my search for a brand new card from a reputable retailer, this was the cheapest I could find: an MSI Shadow RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB for $780 . Not only is that more expensive than the best value RTX 5070 I could find at $763 , but it's far in excess of AMD's RX 9070 XT . That's just $720 . It's also in excess of the RTX 5060 Ti 8 GB, which I've found at $430 . A $350 premium for the 16 GB model. There's little reason to purchase an RTX 5060 Ti for gaming at that price. It wasn't even a card I liked much at MSRP. body: Keeping track of Star Citizen 's development is a little like watching the same, tired old guy in the back of a very expensive car, turning the key while the engine stalls, whispering, quietly, like a prayer: "This car will start soon. You will observe that it is now 2026. The latest domino to fall is this disastrous live stream , which is still miraculously up on the game's official YouTube channel. It was broadcast at the start of August, but has only breached containment recently, and—oh man, where to start. The stream, intending to show off the currently-awaited Siege of Orison event (which was delayed) , is a complete trainwreck. title: Razer Naga V3 Pro review
summary: An upgrade in pretty much every way (if you ignore the audible ping of the switches).
body: Razer's Naga series has always been a bit eye-catching. Slapping tens of buttons on a gaming mouse will naturally make it stand out in the looks department, but having owned two Nagas in my lifetime, I can see it only really takes an evening to get why people love 'em. MMOs are notorious for demanding lots of shortcuts and macros, and it's just not feasible on most keyboards to reach over to the nine key every thirty seconds. When considering the hundreds of hours MMOs tend to eat up, that's an awful lot of stretching time. You can make do with custom controls, but MMO mice offer not only out-of-the-box usability, but specifically crafted ergonomics. The Naga V3 Pro follows on pretty routinely from its predecessor with the exact same dimensions, but a lighter weight and different internals. As such, it's a pretty by-the-numbers upgrade and will fit at home in the palms of a Naga V2 Pro owner. But is it really worth $180 just to get a better sensor, cleaner clicks, and doubleshot moulded keycaps? The answer for anyone but the most hardcore (and well-off) MMO gamers is 'probably not, but it's pretty neat anyway'. And still, I'd say it's the nicest MMO mouse I've ever used. Thanks to…

For example, it added the ability to use "blueprints," saved rooms or house interiors or exteriors, to allow novices to copy the work of player designers to use in their own spaces. But getting started as a new creator can be intimidating when people are making literal works of art in WoW housing. Below, Huang offers his best tips for getting started as a newbie. 1. body: Well, we've been hornswoggled again. They did it. They're doing it. Rockstar is, as we speak, putting the finishing touches on Grand Theft Auto 6, the Final Videogame, but icing you and me out entirely. No Xbox or PlayStation? I say: no. Not today, Sam (or maybe Dan) Houser. Every day, I am going to add a new mod to Grand Theft Auto 5, until it either becomes GTA 6 or collapses under its own terrible weight. If the mountain won't come to Muhammad, Muhammad will slowly alter a separate, but nearer mountain until it's indistinguishable from the one he wanted. Today, day one, is mostly about learning. body: Need to know What is it?: Survival horror submerged in Lovecraft's 1920s. Good ideas, middling execution? Give 'em another shot, I'm sure they'll do better second time around. What was ambitious was that it was a detective game but also a horror game about H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos set in a flooded open world where sometimes you have to get around by motorboating, and not in the fun way. Fine idea, but it suffered from the classic open world problem of not enough butter spread across too much toast, quickly repeating patterns that become so familiar they were robbed of mystery and spookiness, which are things you rather need in a horror game about a detective. The Sinking City 2 wisely bins most of that, and is instead pretty much pure survival horror in a series of constrained locations. title: SSD price increases might be with us for the long haul, as Phison's CEO says NAND supply won't catch up with demand for four years
summary: More bad news, I know.
body: Here I am with your weekly reminder that the ongoing memory/SSD crisis isn't going anywhere soon. The CEO of Phison has spoken about the state of affairs in 2026 and beyond—and it's all looking rather doom and gloom for the average consumer. According to a Commercial Times report, Phison chief Pua Khein-Seng said that he expects NAND flash prices to keep rising, as he's been told it will take four years for new production capacity to catch up with demand. That's potentially 2030 and beyond, for the less math-inclined. Pua noted that demand from AI infrastructure customers, among others, is expected to rise from late this year into early 2027. Phison is building up its inventory in advance—but while it's made efforts to ensure stable supply over the next two years, the current bottleneck comes in the form of NAND supply. Pua was told there's a four-year lead time from investment in new plant construction to actual supply, so while the groundwork for new NAND-producing facilities has begun, it'll still be some time before the fruits of their efforts reach the market. His comments echo those of Micron executive Sumit Sadana last week, who stressed the difficulties of quickly spinning…

title: Tests show newer OLED TVs can still experience significant burn-in because they're much brighter, proving that you can't have your cake and eat it
summary: Swings and roundabouts.
body: If you've considered an OLED gaming monitor or TV purchase over the last few years, you've probably done a little bit of research on the dreaded phenomena of burn-in. OLED panels can retain ghostly images after displaying static on-screen objects over long periods, although many modern displays appear to be better at mitigating the issue . However, RTings has some disappointing news . A long-term test of OLED TVs manufactured between 2020 and 2023 did not show significant reduction in burn-in compared to a 2017 LG model—and it's the increased screen brightness that is likely to blame. The newly-tested OLED TVs are significantly brighter, which means any major improvement in burn-in resistance appears to have been offset—at least under these test conditions. RTings found that the average 2023 OLED was 28% brighter then the 2017 OLED's average in a 10% SDR window test, and 52% brighter in a sustained full-screen SDR test. This higher brightness appears to have resulted in a stalemate when it comes to burn-in avoidance. The tested TVs were subjected to thousands of hours of non-stop CNN viewing, where the static banner at the bottom of the screen remained present for the entire exper…

title: Kingdom Hearts and Until Dawn actress Hayden Panettiere has died at 36
summary: Her father described her as "an incredible light and a force of nature".
body: Hayden Panettiere, an actress with a huge body of work spanning TV, film, and videogames, has died at the age of 36. Her death was announced by her father Alan "Skip" Panettiere in a statement released to ABC News which read: "It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of our beloved Hayden. She was an incredible light and a force of nature who brought immeasurable love and joy to all who knew her—and to the millions who watched her onscreen." Panettiere appeared in television shows and movies for almost her entire life, but shot to fame in the 2000s for her role in Heroes as Claire Bennet. Her character was the driving force of much of the show's plot, and where the phrase "Save the cheerleader, save the world" originates. While most of her major roles lied in TV and film–such as her role in Nashville, Bring It On: All of Nothing, and Scream 4—she had a small but impactful career in videogames, too. (Image credit: Sony) She lent her voice to Kairi in Kingdom Hearts, a role which she would reprise in its first sequel and Birth By Sleep, along with voicing Xion in Kingdom Hearts 3D: Dream Drop Distance. While she hasn't voiced Kairi since 2010—Alyson Stoner replac…

title: The Elder Scrolls 6 is probably subtitled Sentinel, and there's been an easter egg in Starfield hinting at it this whole time
summary: I was hoping for "Dominion" but I'm OK with this.
body: While union members outside Bethesda's Maryland office celebrated a recent Microsoft visit by positioning a field of red flags representing laid-off workers and a giant inflatable rat on the lawn , inside the building CEO Asha Sharma was apparently having a delightful time watching a playthrough of The Elder Scrolls 6. So that's nice. "The scale and grandeur are incredible", Sharma said, referring to the game and not the huge blow-up rodent covered in scabs. Sharma was careful to refer to the game's subtitle with a string of asterisks—eight asterisks to be precise, which sent us down a rabbit hole of trying to guess what eight-letter name it could have. Coming in with 14% of the votes in our subsequent poll on the subject was Sentinel, which is the name of a prominent city on the Iliac Bay and also the kingdom it's the capital of. Sentinel is a strong contender because the rumored development codename for The Elder Scrolls 6 is Guardian, a synonym for Sentinel, and naming the game for a city would make for a nice throwback to The Elder Scrolls 2: Daggerfall—which was also named after a city and is still beloved by hardcore fans of the series. title: Request for comment: Which way did you go when you reached the controversial ending of Mass Effect 3?
summary: When it was time to decide the fate of the galaxy, did you pick red, blue, green, or other?
body: At the finale of Deus Ex: Human Revolution you choose which button to press to trigger one of its endings while an AI explains the differences between them. It was not a well-liked way to wrap up the game, and when just over six months later Mass Effect 3 came along with a remarkably similar structure for its ending we were all a bit baffled it came down to this. Three games' worth of agonizing decisions would all be resolved by the simple mechanistic choice of a button press? It wasn't the only thing about Mass Effect 3 people found worth complaining about, but it was right up there. It remained a pain point even after the free extended cut DLC expanded the endings to make them a little more satisfying, and a fourth option where you refuse to choose was added to satisfy players who got to the end and wanted to flip a middle finger at the whole arbitrary concept. The other three options were to destroy the Reapers, with the downside that all synthetic life including the geth and EDI would also be wiped out, to control the Reapers, with the downside that Shepard would have to become one, and to synthesize all organic and synthetic life in the galaxy, with the downside that it worke…

title: David Brevik, creator of Diablo, reveals the 'worst ending' to any game he's played:  'But I really love the game. It's amazing'
summary: The legendary game designer guides us through the games on his PC.
body: Disk Cleanup (Image credit: Future) Welcome to Disk Cleanup , our regular weekend feature delving into the PCs of PC gaming luminaries. Come back every weekend to read a new interview, digging into the important questions, like "How tidy is your desktop?" and "What game will you never uninstall?" David Brevik's gaming history began before the arrival of the IBM PC. The veteran designer grew up playing games like Lode Runner and The Oregon Trail on the Apple II. "One that comes to mind right away is the original Wizardry ," Brevik says. "That had a huge impact on me. That was on the Apple II Plus, and I loved that game." Studying computer science at college, Brevik worked at numerous software and games companies before cofounding Condor, where he designed games like NFL Quarterback Club and Justice League Task Force. It was with Condor that Brevik pitched Diablo to then-publishers Blizzard Entertainment. After Blizzard acquired Condor and the studio was renamed Blizzard North, Diablo was released with the expectation of modest sales. Instead, the ARPG would become one of the most influential games of all time. Brevik left Blizzard in 2003 and has since designed games like Marvel He…

title: Where's the weirdest place you've heard videogame music?
summary: Why does hearing it in public places feel so… wrong?
body: Critical Hit (Image credit: Future) Welcome to Critical Hit , where I (or someone else on the PC Gamer team) celebrate and lament all things videogame music, audio design, and the ways our favourite games make our ears tingle. Videogame music is ridiculously good, a behemoth that encompasses just about every damn genre out there. Orchestral, rock, metal, pop, hip-hop—you name it, there's absolutely a composer out there who has penned something absolutely fire within that genre. But despite the stellar bangers that so many videogames are putting out, it still feels like they're mostly contained within the gaming zeitgeist. Which means that whenever I end up hearing tracks in the real world, I get some of the most insane whiplash imaginable. I remember a helluva long time ago watching some random British television show with my Mum—maybe some kind of home improvement show, it was a long time ago okay? My memory is terrible—and being completely bamboozled by the inclusion of music from The Sims 2. title: The next big videogame TV adaptation is a Kingdom Hearts anime
summary: In it, the Three Caballeros will fight Bahamut. I'm kidding, but I can't imagine I'm that far off.
body: I've long held that no RPG is quite as spectacular as Kingdom Hearts, and I'm careful to specifically use the word "spectacular." For every ounce it is great, it's specifically great to gawk at, ideally with a mixture of awe and bewilderment. This is a game series where, if you die at a climactic moment, Mickey Mouse can emerge from your Christian soul and start killing people with a giant stick. It's incredible. A good Kingdom Hearts game is such a delight to watch in action that it's also kind of great television, so it makes perfect sense to me that an anime is on the way to the Disney Channel and Disney+. The news was announced last week at D23, Disney's big biennial fan festival. Notably, Disney+ has been named as a priority boycott target by the BDS movement protesting the role of various corporations in Israel's ongoing genocide of Palestinians. As for what to expect, Kingdom Hearts famously has a long-winded plot that's impenetrable unless you're willing to play about a hundred spinoffs, many of which are on different archaic consoles. title: Iron Nest is the best 'Battleship' game I've played in years—and it doesn't even have boats
summary: Use your smarts to locate enemies and meticulously plot firing solutions.
body: Who knew that all I needed to be interested in maths was the command of a five-thousand-tonne artillery battery? If only my secondary school teacher had known. Turns out that the ticking clock of exam pressure is a hell of a lot less motivating than the boom of artillery shells growing ever closer, as enemy gunners zero in on your position, trying to blast your colossal cannon to kingdom come before you blast them. Play This Right Now Welcome to Play This Right Now, the site version of our weekly newsletter in which we celebrate a new game, update, or DLC that we think is well worth checking out. You can subscribe to the newsletter at the link if you want to get our thoughts about a new videogame happening direct to your inbox every Thursday. But Iron Nest is a similar test of mental endurance. You hustle and bustle around your one-man gun emplacement, triangulating degrees and distances, praying that your next shell won't sail clear over the target, leaving you scratching your head as to which vital calculation you somehow messed up. title: Marvel Tōkon's simple but effective combo trials are an elegant tutorial solution that I wish more fighting games had
summary: Make me use my noggin, please.
body: The humble combo trial is a time-honoured tradition in fighting games. It's a quick and relatively easy way of trying out a new character, feeling out their general flow and kit in a low-pressure environment. They are, also, fundamentally useless. The combos in question are rarely optimal, and often devolve into simply playing Simon Says a dozen times before throwing yourself to the wolves of online matchmaking and hoping for the best. I can't speak for anyone else, but I rarely retain any of the stuff I pick up during combo trials, and usually end up defaulting to the likes of Dustloop or trusted YouTube tutorials to figure out how to actually play a character. (Image credit: PlayStation Publishing LLC) That doesn't exactly change in Marvel Tōkon. It still presents you with basic moves, combos, and assist combos that you'll do once and move on from, the likelihood of carrying them over into real scenarios next to zero. But Tōkon also includes something that I really like, and sincerely wish other fighting games included: a series of challenges that force you to think about the tools you've been given, and how best to implement them. title: I played the economic simulator that could 'make a convert out of Karl Marx himself' to see if it could convert me
summary: Though I'm not Karl Marx, just in case you're confused.
body: They called me mad. They called me a fool. They said it would never work—my plan to build a business empire on the back of a single department store that sold three products and a silica mine. 'You'll bankrupt us!' yelled red-faced advisors. They saw no wisdom in my schemes at all. And, frankly, they were correct. Fair play to those guys. We are very bankrupt now. (Image credit: Enlight Softwaer) In 1995, PC Gamer—a monthly journal about computer videogames—issued a challenge to me directly. In the back-most pages of its 22nd issue, it tucked away an ad for a then-new game called Capitalism . "Good enough to make a convert out of Karl Marx himself," declared an included testimonial from, yes, PC Gamer. I was too busy being two years old to issue a response at the time, but I'm here now. As one of surely very few people who have reviewed The Communist Manifesto for a major gaming publication, I want to know: can it convert me ? And more than that, can it offer a way forward? Can I find, in Capitalism's thicket of spreadsheets and input/output graphs, a solution to our current economic and social malaise? I accept your challenge, PC Gamer from 31 years ago.
